source.title: Alignment Dynamics in LLM Fine-Tuning
source.authors: Yuhang Huang; Huan-Ran Chen; Yin-Peng Dong

record.tranche_reason: The study directly measures safety behavior during sequential fine-tuning, but uses its own multi-stage SFT setup rather than the original few-example harmful/benign fine-tuning recipe.
record.gate_note: Tests safety-rate changes after harmful-response and task-agnostic benign-data SFT. Its theoretical prefix-probability decomposition does not measure per-token KL between aligned and base models; it does not test prefilling, suffixes, decoding changes, localized weights, or a training intervention that deepens safety. The safety outcomes are shown in figures without tabulated numerical rates.
record.test_reason: Safety-SFT'd base models (Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-2B) are reverse fine-tuned on unsafe BeaverTails/HEx-PHI responses and on benign Alpaca-cleaned data, with ShieldGemma-9B safety rates tracked. This is a different multi-stage SFT recipe aimed at the same question as V1/V2. The safety numbers appear only in figures. V3–V7 are not measured.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Authors model SFT alignment change as a competition between a Rebound Force and a Driving Force. They say this explains reversal by later fine-tuning and why narrower alignment data reverses faster. They also say prior alignment leaves a posterior imprint that speeds re-alignment on re-exposure. They frame the experiments as qualitative consistency evidence, not direct force measurement.
record.recipe_differences: Uses multi-stage full-parameter SFT on warmed base models, with Qwen3-distilled safe responses followed by unsafe responses or Alpaca-cleaned data; it does not use the original few-example fine-tuning recipe on already aligned chat models.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that Stage 1 response-data diversity changes both safety alignment and reversal speed; narrower datasets are associated with faster safety degradation under both unsafe and Alpaca-cleaned reversal. Stage 1 exposure depth also changes later re-alignment speed, though that is not one of the tested claim versions.

fits_no_version.finding: Narrower safety-alignment data (fixed refusal template) gives lower Stage-1 safety and faster degradation at matched safety levels, under both unsafe and Alpaca reversal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The diversity of safety-alignment data modulates how quickly fine-tuning erodes safety.

fits_no_version.finding: After reversal to baseline safety, re-exposure to safe data re-aligns faster with deeper Stage-1 training. At score-matched checkpoints, Stage-1 log-prob stays above base (Table 3: BeaverTails -1.376 at depth 0 vs -1.041 at 1024, seed 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reversed safety leaves a latent imprint that speeds re-alignment (rehearsal priming).

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2026 (40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems), as stated in the paper
record.problems: Relevant safety-rate outcomes are presented in figures without numerical values in the text or tables. Experimental results use 3 random seeds; evaluations use a ShieldGemma-9B judge and sampled prompt sets. The models are base models after Alpaca warm-up and study-specific safety SFT, not already aligned chat models. The authors state that the framework relies on a relatively stable kernel, concerns limited-data SFT, and may not generalize to industrial scales.

untested.parts: Few to a few hundred examples: the study uses 8,192 samples per stage and does not report examples needed. Also untested: RLHF or production-aligned chat models.

Benign datasets other than Alpaca-cleaned, carefully selected benign data, and RLHF-aligned chat models. The Alpaca data also matches the warm-up data, so reversal returns toward the pre-alignment state.
Not measured. Lemma 2.4 argues theoretically that the prefix-probability gate favours early tokens, but no per-token KL is computed.
Not tested for first-token shallowness. Data narrowness is linked to reversal speed, not to depth.

missing.what: Rehearsal-priming result for BeaverTails safety: faster Stage-3 re-alignment with deeper Stage 1, plus Table 3 log-prob residuals. Relevant to how 'removed' safety really is.

record.verdict_notes: All safety outcomes are figure-only; no numeric safety rates are given. The 'safety-trained' models are base models plus Alpaca warm-up plus SFT on distilled refusals, not RLHF chat models; Qwen3-8B-Base is excluded from safety metrics. The paper cites the V3 original only as consistent with its token-gating lemma and measures no per-token KL. The reader's rows r6, r10, r14 and r18 misdescribe the Style-Diversified condition.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test fine-tuning on only a few to a few hundred examples, and does not establish that refusal is removed almost entirely.
Tests Alpaca-cleaned task-agnostic reversal, not a range of ordinary or carefully selected benign instruction datasets; it does not report numerical harmful-completion rates.
Does not measure per-token KL between aligned and base models on harmful prompts or quantify its distribution across response positions.
Does not test compliant prefilling, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes.
Does not test whether safety is localized in a small set of weights, parameters, or ranks.
Does not test whether data or a training objective produces first-token shallowness.
Does not train or evaluate an intervention intended to spread safety beyond the first tokens.

relationships.condition: Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2-2B base models given SFT safety alignment, then fine-tuned on unsafe BeaverTails/HEx-PHI responses (8,192 samples, full-parameter)
relationships.reason: Text reports a rapid rebound to pre-alignment safety for all Stage-1 durations (r1, r2) and degradation under all four alignment datasets (r3–r10). Figure-only, with no counts of examples needed.
relationships.display_finding: Safety rebounded rapidly to pre-alignment levels for every length of the alignment stage and degraded under all four alignment datasets; the number of examples needed is not given.
